blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a large-scale study into lateral phishing attacks, where compromised accounts within an organization are used to send phishing emails to other employees. The paper, conducted with Barracuda Networks, analyzes 113 million emails from 230K mailboxes across 92 organizations to detect and characterize these attacks. The authors develop a Random Forest classifier with an 87.3% detection rate and a minimal false positive rate (0.00036%) to identify phishing emails, using features like recipient count, historical recipient similarity, phishing keywords, and URL reputation. Key findings include the prevalence of lateral phishing (101K mailboxes received at least one such email), the success rate of account takeovers (11% leading to further compromises), and the generic nature of attack strategies (e.g., mass emails, generic subject lines). Attackers often use simple lures like account alerts or shared documents and operate during normal working hours. The study reveals that attackers prioritize volume over sophistication, suggesting their current methods are economically viable.
paper_title: Detecting and characterizing lateral phishing at scale
paper_abstract: We present the first large-scale characterization of lateral phishing attacks, based on a dataset of 113 million employeesent emails from 92 enterprise organizations. In a lateral phishing attack, adversaries leverage a compromised enterprise account to send phishing emails to other users, benefitting from both the implicit trust and the information in the hijacked user’s account. We develop a classifier that finds hundreds of real-world lateral phishing emails, while generating under four false positives per every one-million employeesent emails. Drawing on the attacks we detect, as well as a corpus of user-reported incidents, we quantify the scale of lateral phishing, identify several thematic content and recipient targeting strategies that attackers follow, illuminate two types of sophisticated behaviors that attackers exhibit, and estimate the success rate of these attacks. Collectively, these results expand our mental models of the ‘enterprise attacker’ and shed light on the current state of enterprise phishing attacks.
